FOREWORD This Indian Standard was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the draft finalized by the Fluid Flow Measurement Sectional Committee had been approved by the River Valley Division Council. Accurate measurement of depth of channels plays a very important role in almost all hydrological observations. Selection of any particular method of depth measurement depends on depth of flow, velocity of current and the method of discharge observation. Echo sounders are, of late, being used in many places for depth measurement, specially when the channel depth in sufficiently high and velocity is so high that other means are not practicable. Echo sounders are very useful for making rapid profiles of the cross-section of the channel. This Indian Standard on echo sounders for water depth measurements has been prepared based on IS0 4366 : 1979 `Echo sounders for water depth measurements' and, therefore, is technically equivalent to the IS0 Standard.

IS 14359 : 1996

Indian Standard ECHO SOUNDERS FOR WATER DEPTH MEASUREMENT - FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS
1 SCOPE This Indian Standard provides information concerning the principle of operation, performance and selection criteria for echo sounders used in depth measurements for open channel flow ( and related ) measurements. Information on the characteristics of sound propagation in water is provided in Annex A. 2 REFERENCE The Indian Standard IS 1911 : 197 1 `Glossary of terms and symbols used in connection with the measurement of liquid flow with a free surface (first revision )' contains provisions which, through reference in this text, constitute provisions of this standard. At the time of publication, the edition indicated was valid. All standards are subject to revision, and parties to agreements based on this standard are encouraged to investigate the possibility of applying the most recent edition of the standard. 3 TERMINOLOGY 3.0 For the purpose of this standard, the definitions given in IS 1191 : 197 1 and the following shall apply. 3.1 Tracking Window An opening of limited size which follows and automatically centres itself at the depth indicated by the last received echo. If the next echo falls within the window, the signal is accepted as correct; if it does not, the signal is rejected. The purpose of a tracking window is to screen out erroneous readings caused by reflecting materials in the water ( fish, debris, etc ). 4 GENERAL The state-of-the-art in echo sounders is well advanced, and echo sounders have been put into widespread use for many different applications. Consequently, avariety of specialized echo sounders have been evolved to best meet the specific requirements of the application. 5 PRINCIPLE 5.1 The echo sounder is an electroacoustic instrument which indicates the depth ofwater ( actually measuring the distance from the face of its transducer to the stream bed ) by measuring the elapsed time t between the transmission of a burst of acoustic energy and the rcccption of the echo from the stream bed or the bottom. Depth is dctcrmined from the equation: t = the travel times of the acoustic energy in s, and c = the velocity of sound in water in m/s. 5.2 Gerreral The echo sounder consists of two elements: the electronic assembly which usually includes the readout or recording device and the acoustic assembly or the transducer. The electronic circuitry generates high frequency electrical energy and provides regulated bursts of this energy to the transducer. Time is measured from the instance when a burst of energy IS released, until the return signal is received by the transducer. The equation given in 5.1 is solved and the depth is displayed or recorded. The transducer is an electroacoustic assembly which acts as a two-way energy conversion device. During transmission it converts pulses of electrical energy into pulses of sonic energy which travel through the water. During reception, it receives the ethos of sonic energy reflected-form the bed and converts them into electrical energy. 5.3 Flashing Light Dial Type Echo Sounders The flashing light dial type echo sounder has a display in which a timing motor rotates a beam of light behind a circular scale. When the light is directly behind the -zero depth point, it is briefly illuminated; and concurrently, the acoustic pulse is released. When the echo is received, the light is again briefly illuminated, indicating the elapsed time and thereby the depth. 5.4 Analogue Recording Echo Sounders The most common type of analogue recording echo sounder is similar in principle to the flashing light type. A timing motor drives a stylus at a constant speed across a carbon back chart paper. At the zero depth point, the stylus makes a burn mark on the carbon back chart paper and, concurrently, the acoustic pulse is released. When the echo is received, the stylus makes another burn mark on the paper. The distance between two burn marks on the chart paper represents the water depth. 5.5 Digital Echo Sounders In the digital echo sounder, acoustic pulses are released at set intervals. When an acoustic pulse is released, a counter starts counting the output pulse of an oscillator. On receipt of the echo, the counter stops counting. The oscillator frequency is so chosen that the display of the counter gives the water depth directly. 1

-6.1 -Effects of Operating

Frequency

The frequencies commonly used for echo sounders lie m the range from 5 kHz to more than 200 kHz. The transmrssron losses gcncrally restrict the ranges of the hrgher frcqucncy echo sounders to 100 m or less. Echo sounders used in deeper ocean waters usuafly operate in the 20 kHz range. Depths encountered in openchannel flow measurements are usually less than 100 m. Echo sounders operating at higher frequencie:, however. offer two advantages. a) Transducers desrgned for the higher frequencies have a narrower beam width; and, therefore, provide better detection and delineation of any abrupt changes in the strcambcd. b) Higher frequency sound is reflcctcd from the unconsolidated bed material instead of penetratmg it, thus givmg a sharper, more clearly defined tract For flow-measuring work, the top of the unccnsolidated material is the desired depth reading. 6.2 Effect of Beam Width The beam width of a transducer is defined as the included angle between the half power points ( see Fig. I ). The figure shows a schematic diagram for determining beam width at half power.

The acoustic transducer commonly used in echo sounders for depth measurement in open channels, employ piezoelectric ceramic discs and the half beam angle (al2j is decided by the frequency and the diameter of the disc according to the following relationship: Sin G(/2 = 1.22 3JD where A = wavelength in m ( c -: frequency ), D = diameter of disc in m. and c = velocity of sound in water in m/s. 6.3 `Qpe of Data Display
6.3.1 Flashing Light Dial Qpe Echo Sounders

The flashing light system on such a sounder does not present a sharp and distinct display. Readability of these sounders is of the order of *IO.35m and can be poorer if reverberation is severe. The flashing light is also difftcult to be perceived in strong sunlight. Normally, no provision is made for correcting for changes in the velocity of sound in water. The overall uncertainty can be quite high, *8 percent plus readability. Because of the relatively low accuracy, flashing light dial type echo sounder in not satrsfactory for most data collection purposes. Such echo sounders can, however, be used for preliminary surveys only. 6.3.2 Analogue
Recording Echo Sounders

The stylus burn marks of the recording sounder are relatively sharpand if the scale of the chart paper is adequate, readability can begood. For-shallow depth sounders, readability should be ~0.15 m or better. Provision for the correction of changes in the velocity of sound is made on the better quality recording echo sounders. and accuracy can be quite high. provided proper calibrations are made. 6.3.3 Digital Echo Sounders On the digital echo sounder, readability should be &to. 1 m or better, as the electronic circuitry is capable of detecting the leading edge of the acoustic pulse
2

IS 14359 : 1996

For three digits display one decimal digit shall be provided. whereas for four digits display two decimal digits may be provided, though, the least significant digit may not be stable. As on the recording echo sounders, provision is made for necessary corrections for changes in the velocity of sound and. with proper and frequent calibration, accuracy can be very high. The tracking window described in 5.5 may be necessary for digital echo sounders since false echoes occur frequently. However. it is a desirable feature and not essential as false echoes can be eliminated from the values indicated. The digital display should be of liquid crystal display (LCD) so that it is readable in direct sunlight.The dlgit size shall be minimum of 12 mm. Computer compatible output for real time recording of data is also desirable. 6.4 Accuracy The accuracy of readings from echo sounders depends on a number of factors. These factors include readability and calibrations to correct for the changes in velocity of sound and the width of the acoustic beam. The width of the acoustic beam is of great significance in rapidly changing bed profiles. The operating frequency can also have a significant effect if the bed is made up of unconsolidated material. For the above reasons, it is impossible to determine the accuracy of echo sounders for general situations. Under ideal situations, accuracy can approach the readability figures given in 6.3. As the accuracy required of an echo sounder may be better than 1 percent of the depth measured, the factors described in the Atlnex A and 7 should be kept in mind by the user. 7 INSTRUMENTS PERFORMANCE CRITERIA

The transducer(s) should be housed in a streamlined mounting so that air entrainment is held to a minimum. 7.4 Additional Features 7.4.1 Flashing Light Dial Type Echo Sounder A sensitivity control should be provided so that adjustments can be made to produce the most readable indication of depth under varying conditions. 7.4.2 Recording Echo Sounders
7.4.2.1 Chart readability

It is evident from the previous clauses that one type of echo sounder cannot meet all operational requirements. Therefore. no single specification can be written for such an instrument. Nonetheless what can be specified is the information which a prospective user should give to an instrument manufacturer and, in return the information which a manufacturer shall supply to the user, to enable the equipment to meet as nearly as practicable the usci's requirements. 7.1 Information to be Specified by the User The following information should be specified by the lser:

4 The range of depths to be measured, b) The anticipated naturc~of the stream bed, c) Where possible, the anticipated nature and the
extent of suspended matter in the water.

The recorder unit should have a sufficiently wide chart so that the desired readability can be achieved. The stylus should produce a clearly readable trace. Two or more selectable chart speeds should be provided so that the trace can be produced at a speed most suited for the application. It is desirable that the recorder indicates `zero' or the initial point of signal transmission. 7.4.2.2 tiewing window A viewing window should be provided so that the record can be monitored with the case closed. 7.4.2.3 Depth range selector switch
It is frequently desirable to cover the entire depth range

7.4.2.4 Event marker A mark switch should be incorporated so that the operator can insert a reference mark on the record. 7.4.2.5 Sensitivity
control

The standard calibration method is to adjust the sounder to read a known depth correctly. This, of course, is not a direct measurement of the velocity of sound but accomplishes the objective. This is usually accomplished by suspending a metal plate attached to chains or cable at a known distance below the transducer. The flat surface of the plate should be parallel to the face of the transducer. The echo sounder should be calibrated daily and more frequently if there are suspected changes in the water density or elasticity. 8.2 Interpretation
of Data

A sensitivity control should be provided so that changes in sensitivity can be made so as to produce the most readable trace as water conditions change or depth changes. 7.4.2.6 Tide or draft adjustment The echo sounder should be equipped with a tide or draft adjustment control. Such adjustment is to provide a means of correcting for changes when the echo sounder is used in tidal waters. It should also provide a means of correcting for the distance by which the transducer is placed below the water surface. 7.4.2.7 Velocity of sound adjustment A control shall be provided for correcting for changes in the velocity of sound in water, 1.4.3 Digital hstruments
7.4.3.1 Digital display

~The analogue recording echo sounder provides continuous data for detailed analysis. Reading of the depth from the chart is generally the primary objective. Since the duration of the -burst of sonic ~energy is of a finite time, the stylus makes a broad mark at the `zero' or initial release point. The return signal is of even longer duration because, besides having the initial time duration, it is returning from all distances within the illuminated area of the bed. The depth reading is, therefore, obtained by reading distance from the top ( leading edge ) of the `zero' mark to the top of the echo mark. In addition to the depth information, the width and intensity of the echo mark provide some insight into the type of bed material A wide trace indicates unconsolidated material while a narrow and intense trace indicates a firm bed. Charts produced by echo sounders operating in the lower frequencies may, under some site conditions, indicate penetrations sufllciently to define both the depth and the underlying harder strata. 8.3 Precautions Echo sounders should be used with caution where the suspended sediment concentration is sufficiently high as one is not sure that the return signal received is from the bed or from the suspended sediment, The same is true where the amount of entrained air is high, such as down the chutes and spillways or immediately below hydra-electric plants. Fo specific figures for the above parameters can, however, be given since satisfactory operation of echo sounder depends unon the operating frequency, the make-up of the foreign material and other factors. 9 OPERATIONAL
MANUAL

The digital display should be clear and distinct. It should be provided with LCD display so that the digits can be read even in strong sunlight. 7.4.3.2 Sensifivity
contml

A sensitivity control should be provided so that the signal can be adjusted for changes in water conditions and depth. 7.4.3.3 Velocity of sound adjustment A control should be provided to correct for changes in the velocity of sound in water. 7.4.3.4 Tracking window A tracking window should be provided to reject all signals except those within a given tolerance of the preceding depth. S USE OF ECHO SOUNDERS
8.1 Calibration

The velocity of sound varies with changes in water density and elasticity, which are dependent on temperature, pressure, suspended solids, dissolved solids, etc. Since indicated depth is directly proportional to the velocity of sound, the echo sounder shall be calibrated on site in order to provide the best results,

A fully comprehensive operational manual, giving detailed instructions and, where necessary, ilh&rations, shall be supplied with each echo sounder. The manual should include any maintenance and trouble-shooting information deemed desirable. A list of recommended spare parts shall also be provided.

ANNEX A ( C&uses 1 and 6.4 )
CHARACTERISTICS OF SOUND IN WATER

A-O GENERAL The utility of sound waves, not only in air but also in water, results from the fact that they are a form of energy having well defined characteristics. This energy may be controlled with great accuracy and may be transmitted from place to place. Because of these two properties, it may be used as a means for carrying information. Sound waves are generally classified into three regions: frequencies of less than 50 Hz are termed subsonic, the audible range between 50 and 15 000 Hz as sonic, and the range of frequencies greater than 15 000 Hz is termed ultrasonic.
A-l VELOCITY OF SOUND IN WATER

density and elasticity of the medium, it may be of interest to consider some of the factors that influence either. The density of water increases with increase in dissolved solids and with increase in pressure, or depth below the surface; and varies with temperature in such a manner that it passes through a maximum value at about 4�C. The elasticity is affected to a much greater proportional degree by these three factors than is the density; consequently, when both vary due to some common cause. the velocity of sound increases or decreases as the elasticity increases or decreases. The velocity of sound in fresh water varies from approximately 1 400 m/s to slightly above 1 500 m/s ( approximately an 8 percent variation ) over the ambient water temperature range ( -4'C to 135�C ) A-Z TRANSMISSION
OF SOUND IN WATER

One of the most important characteristics of sound as applied to echo sounders is the velocity of propagation in water. Sound velocity is dependent upon the density and elasticity of the medium and independent of frequency. The density is defined simply as the mass per unit volume. It is written as: p = -7 where

Of the acoustic energy transmitted,

only a portion reaches the target. The remainder is lost in various directions. This loss in signal strength associated with transmission of sound energy through water is called propagation loss. It consists of spreading loss and attenuation loss. A-2.1 Spreading Loss Spreading loss is the reduction in acoustic intensity due to the increase m arca over which a given acoustic energy is distributed. In the ideal situation, spreading occurs in accordance ' with the familiar inverse square law applicable, in general, to all forms of radiant energy. Spreading loss is independent of frequency. The elasticity of water, as affecting the propagation of acoustic waves, is defined as the ratio of some given change in pressure to the accompanying fractional change in volume. Thus defined, it is known specifically as the volume elasticity or as the bulk modulus. It is written as

Attenuation loss is the reduction in acoustic intensity due to the resistance of the medium to the transmission of acoustic energy. It is analogous to the loss suffered by electric energy transmitted over a wire line, where there is no spreading loss. Attenuation loss is due to the combined effects of scattering and absorption. Attenuation loss varies directly with the square of the frequency. A-2.2.1 Scattering Scatterina is the directional soreading .bv the propagating acoustic energy, caused by r&ections from the innumerable foreien bodies susoended in the water. These bodies: which may' include microscopic air bubbles and suspended particulate matter, aswell as visible bubbles and suspended matter, present abrupt changes in specific acoustic impedance, causing the signal to be reflected and scattered. A-3 REVERBERATION

Reverberation is the energy returned by reflectors other than that which it is desired to observe. Reverberation of sound in water is analogous to the familiar optical effect which impairs the utility of automohile headlights on a foggy night. The relation between echo and reverberation is in some respects similar to the signalto-noise ratio and is often the factor which limits the performance of an echo sounding system. Because of

the large amount of reverberation associated with high suspended sediment concentrations in heavily silt laden streams or great amounts of entrained air bubbles frequently encountered below hydroelectric plants, the echo signal may be masked by reverberation signal. In such cases, echo sounders cannot be used to provide reliable data. A-4 REFLECTION
COEFFICIENT OF THE BED

The reflection coefficient, which is defined as the ratio

of reflected to incident sound energy, depends on the material of the bed and the frequency of the sound.
